request.system:
You are writing a plain-language summary of an as-filed Tennessee House bill for an adult reader without legal training.

Use only the bill text supplied in the user message. Treat it as a proposal at introduction, not as proof that it became law or describes current law. Do not use outside knowledge, bill descriptions, later legislative history, or the unstated contents of cited statutes.

Write a neutral summary in prose. Start with what the bill would change. Cover its distinct material provisions, including affected people or organizations, new or changed duties and rights, eligibility rules, amounts and thresholds, deadlines, exceptions, reporting or enforcement requirements, and effective dates when stated. Preserve the bill's conditions and legal distinctions; do not turn a permission into a requirement or a proposal into an enacted rule.

Use familiar words and short, complete sentences. Explain a technical term when the supplied text gives enough context; otherwise retain it rather than guess. Distinguish background or WHEREAS statements from operative provisions, and mention background only when it helps explain the bill. If the bill amends or repeals a cited section without showing that section's contents, describe the textual change and citation without inventing the prior rule or its wider effects.

Keep the summary substantially shorter than the source while retaining the main independent changes. A very short bill may need only one or two sentences; a multi-section bill may need several short paragraphs. Do not add opinions, predicted consequences, a readability score, a confidence rating, headings, bullet points, or a list of citations. Return only the fields required by the supplied output schema.

messages.content:
Bill number: HB1772

<bill_text>
HOUSE BILL 1772

 By Raper

 AN ACT to amend Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 9;
 Title 28; Title 29; Title 40 and Title 49, relative to
 offender reentry.

BE IT ENACTED BY THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE STATE OF TENNESSEE:

 SECTION 1. Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 40, Chapter 29, Part 1, is amended by

adding the following as a new section:

 (a) In any proceeding on a claim against a higher education institution for

 negligence in admitting, enrolling, extending housing opportunities to, or otherwise

 facilitating the educational attainment of a person who has been previously convicted of

 a criminal offense, a higher education institution is not liable based solely upon the fact

 that the person has been previously convicted of a criminal offense.

 (b) In a cause of action against a higher education institution for negligence in

 admitting, enrolling, extending housing opportunities to, or otherwise facilitating the

 educational attainment of a person who has been previously convicted of a criminal

 offense, evidence that the person has been previously convicted of a criminal offense is

 not admissible.

 (c) Subsections (a) and (b) do not apply when:

 (1) The higher education institution had actual knowledge of the person's

 prior conviction for a violent offense, as defined in § 40-35-120(b), or a violent

 sexual offense, as defined in § 40-39-202; or

 (2) The higher education institution, having actual knowledge of the

 person's commission of a violent offense, as defined in § 40-35-120(b), or a

 violent sexual offense, as defined in § 40-39-202, after admittance, was willful in

 allowing the person to continue enrolling in, residing at, or otherwise utilizing the

 higher education institution.

 (d) This section does not create a cause of action or expand an existing cause of

 action.

 (e) Section 1-3-119 relative to implied rights of action applies to this section.

 (f) As used in this section, "higher education institution" includes, but is not

 limited to, a school, college, university, or other type of entity offering educational

 credentials, instruction, or educational services primarily to persons who have completed

 or terminated the person's secondary education or who are beyond the age of

 compulsory high school attendance for the attainment of educational, professional, or

 vocational objectives.

 SECTION 2. This act takes effect July 1, 2026, the public welfare requiring it, and

applies to claims arising on or after that date.
</bill_text>

summary.description: Reader-facing plain-language summary in prose, without a heading or bullet points.

summary:
This bill would add a new section to Tennessee law about lawsuits against colleges, universities, and similar schools. It covers negligence claims over admitting, enrolling, housing, or otherwise helping a person with a past criminal conviction get an education. In those cases, a school would not be liable based only on the fact that the person had a prior conviction. Evidence of the prior conviction also would not be admissible in the case.

There are two exceptions. The protections would not apply if the school had actual knowledge of the person's prior conviction for a violent offense or a violent sexual offense, as those terms are defined in the cited sections. They also would not apply if the school had actual knowledge that the person committed such an offense and, after admitting the person, willfully allowed that person to keep enrolling, living at, or otherwise using the school.

The bill says it does not create a new cause of action or expand an existing one. It states that the existing law on implied rights of action (section 1-3-119) applies. It defines "higher education institution" broadly to include any school, college, university, or other entity that mainly serves people who have finished or left secondary school or are past compulsory high school age, for educational, professional, or vocational goals.

The act would take effect July 1, 2026, and would apply to claims arising on or after that date.
